reference.source: Brocklehurst's Textbook of Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology
clinicalPearls: Decline is defined by loss of basic and instrumental activities of daily living, so quantify it with validated scales rather than relying on diagnoses alone.
An abrupt functional decline is frequently the sole presenting sign of acute illness such as infection or myocardial infarction in older adults, and should be treated as a red flag.
Hospital-associated deconditioning develops within days of bed rest, so early mobilisation and removal of tethers such as catheters and lines are preventive.
Frailty, sarcopenia and disability are overlapping but distinct constructs that guide different interventions.
Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces functional decline and institutionalisation.
Correctable contributors such as visual and hearing impairment, foot problems and home hazards are easily overlooked.
Progressive resistance exercise combined with adequate protein intake can reverse sarcopenia even in the very old.
Always screen for reversible drivers including depression, polypharmacy, pain, malnutrition and undertreated chronic disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Age-related functional decline is the progressive loss of ability to perform activities of daily living arising from the interaction of ageing physiology and superimposed disease. Intrinsic changes include sarcopenia, reduced aerobic capacity and physiological reserve, and sensory decline, which lower the threshold at which stressors overwhelm capacity. Chronic multimorbidity and frailty erode reserve further, while acute precipitants such as illness, hospitalisation, enforced immobility and iatrogenesis trigger rapid deconditioning. Much of the observed decline reflects modifiable disease and inactivity rather than intrinsic ageing, which is why distinguishing usual from successful ageing matters and why targeted intervention can alter the trajectory.
additionalDifferentials: occult infection or other acute illness
additionalInvestigations: functional scales such as the Barthel Index, Lawton instrumental scale, gait speed and Timed Up and Go
frailty assessment using the Fried phenotype or Clinical Frailty Scale
full blood count, urea and electrolytes and thyroid function
vitamin D and vitamin B12 levels
medication review with physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessment
redFlags: abrupt or stepwise decline suggesting acute illness or stroke
safeguarding concerns such as neglect or an unsafe home environment
reference.prognosis: Functional decline predicts falls, hospitalisation, institutionalisation and death, but multicomponent interventions combining exercise, nutrition and comprehensive geriatric assessment can slow, halt or partially reverse it, particularly when precipitants are addressed early.
pitfalls: attributing acute decline to old age and missing an underlying acute illness
prescribing bed rest and promoting deconditioning
overlooking sensory impairment and environmental hazards
failing to set realistic patient-centred functional goals
not reassessing function after a hospital admission
